summary: This article covers a tour of Earth's seven continents, how they differ in size and location, and why the planet's land ended up divided this way.
introduce: Draw two overlapping circles on the board and quickly compare two familiar things, such as a cat and a dog, with the class. Tell students that while reading “Continents: Earth's Big Landmasses” they will look for ways things are alike and different.

keyTerms.def: a large area of land, such as a continent
one half of the Earth, usually divided by the equator or another line
to move slowly, often without being directly pushed

challengeTerms.def: relating to the huge moving plates of rock that make up Earth's outer layer
the name scientists give to the single supercontinent that most of today's continents were once joined in
a huge landmass made up of most or all of Earth's continents joined together

discussion: Do you agree or disagree that it would be exciting to live on a continent with no permanent population, like Antarctica? Use evidence from the article to explain.
Explain how Europe and Asia are connected, and how Australia's location makes it different from most other continents.
struggling: Read the first part of the article aloud together, review landmass, hemisphere, and drift, and let weak readers fill in a T-chart of alike and different with sentence starters.
gifted: Ask strong readers to read a challenging version and write a short paragraph that uses tectonic, Pangaea, and supercontinent to compare two ideas from the article and explain which difference matters most.
